extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (and math contest enthusiasts)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository chapter material introducing group homomorphisms, quotient groups, and the basic theory of rings and ideals, with definitions, examples, and exercises aimed at undergraduate students and contest training. Also includes small topology/continuity exercises at the start of the chunk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgroup generated by a set (⟨S⟩)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let S be a subset of G. The subgroup generated by S, denoted ⟨S⟩, is the set of elements which can be written as a finite product of elements in S (and their inverses). If ⟨S⟩ = G then S is a set of generators for G.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and explanation: for a single element x this gives ... , for two elements x,y this gives all finite words in x,x^{-1},y,y^{-1}. Note: in a finite group the 'and their inverses' clause is unnecessary (exercise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Group presentation (generators and relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A way to describe a group by listing generators and relations between them, typically written ⟨generators | relations⟩.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentations give a compact way to write groups, but the same group can have very different presentations (examples: Z, Z/100Z, dihedral groups). Warning: equality problem for presentations can be undecidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of group homomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Let G = (G,⋆) and H = (H,∗) be groups. A group homomorphism is a map ϕ : G → H such that for any g1,g2 ∈ G we have ϕ(g1 ⋆ g2) = ϕ(g1) ∗ ϕ(g2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: identity map, trivial homomorphism, natural maps Z→Z/nZ, embedding Sn→Sn+1, maps determined by images of generators (must satisfy relations). Important remark: an isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kernel of a homomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: For a homomorphism ϕ : G → H, ker ϕ := {g ∈ G : ϕ(g) = 1_H}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ker ϕ is a subgroup of G. Proposition: ϕ is injective iff ker ϕ = {1_G}. Examples of kernels are given (trivial homomorphism has kernel G; mod n map Z→Z/nZ has kernel nZ; embeddings have trivial kernel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Image of a homomorphism is a subgroup
rubrics_metrics.description: For any homomorphism ϕ : G → H, the image ϕimg(G) is a subgroup of H.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We are especially interested in surjective homomorphisms (images equal whole codomain). Specifying a homomorphism from a presented group requires sending generators to elements of H satisfying relations so the map is well-defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Left coset and equivalence relation for quotient
rubrics_metrics.description: Given subgroup N ⊆ G, define relation g1 ∼_N g2 iff g1 = g2 n for some n∈N. The equivalence class containing g is gN := {g n | n∈N}, called a left coset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cosets partition G and all cosets have the same cardinality. Elements of quotient groups will be these cosets; in practice one often pictures them as representatives (e.g., Z/nZ as {0,...,n-1}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotient group G/N and coset multiplication
rubrics_metrics.description: If N ⊴ G (normal), the quotient group G/N has elements the left cosets of N with product defined by (g1N)·(g2N) := (g1g2)N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction gives a group naturally isomorphic to the codomain Q when N = ker ϕ for a surjective homomorphism ϕ : G ↠ Q. Picture: collapse each coset (fiber) to a point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/criterion for normal subgroup (N ⊴ G)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subgroup N is normal (written N ⊴ G) if it is the kernel of some homomorphism. Equivalently, for every g∈G and h∈N we have g h g^{-1} ∈ N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The equivalence is Theorem 3.5.4: the conjugation condition guarantees well-defined coset multiplication. Example of non-normal subgroup provided (H={1,s} in D12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lagrange's theorem (finite group)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let G be finite and H a subgroup. Then |H| divides |G|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: cosets of H form a partition and all have equal size, so |G| = n·|H|. Consequence: for finite G and normal N, |G/N| = |G|/|N|.

rubrics_metrics.name: First isomorphism theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ϕ : G → H be a homomorphism. Then G / ker ϕ is isomorphic to ϕimg(G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: the quotient by kernel 'collapses' fibers to produce the image; if ϕ is injective the image is an isomorphic copy of G inside H (an embedding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a ring (with 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A ring is a triple (R,+,×) where (R,+) is an abelian group with identity 0, × is an associative binary operation with identity 1, and multiplication distributes over addition. Ring is commutative if × is commutative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's convention: 'ring' means ring with 1. Examples: Z, Q, R, C, polynomial rings R[x], product rings R×S, Gaussian integers Z[i], etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit and field
rubrics_metrics.description: A unit of a ring R is an element u with multiplicative inverse. A nontrivial commutative ring is a field if every nonzero element is a unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: units of Z are ±1; Q,R,C are fields; Z/pZ for prime p is a field. The trivial ring 0 is not a field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of ring homomorphism (preserve 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A ring homomorphism ϕ : R → S satisfies ϕ(x+y)=ϕ(x)+ϕ(y), ϕ(x·y)=ϕ(x)·ϕ(y), and ϕ(1_R)=1_S. If bijective, it's a ring isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: requiring 1↦1 excludes some maps you might expect (e.g., x↦2x on Z is not a ring homomorphism). Examples and non-examples given (no homomorphism Z/2016Z→Z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kernel of ring homomorphism and ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: For ϕ : R → S, ker ϕ := {r∈R : ϕ(r)=0}. A subset I⊆R is an ideal iff it is closed under addition and for every x∈I and r∈R we have r x ∈ I (absorbs multiplication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to normal subgroups: I is kernel of some homomorphism iff I is an ideal (Theorem 4.6.6). The quotient ring R/I is formed from cosets r+I with well-defined addition and multiplication (mod I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotient ring R/I
rubrics_metrics.description: Given ideal I⊊R, R/I := {r + I | r ∈ R} with addition and multiplication induced by representatives; this yields a ring and the natural surjection R ↠ R/I has kernel I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: R/I is what you get when you declare elements of I to be zero (e.g., Z/5Z). Verifying well-defined multiplication uses the absorption property of ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper ideal characterization (no units)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal I ⊆ R is proper (I ≠ R) iff I contains no units of R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: if I contains a unit u then 1=u u^{-1}∈I so I=R. Consequence: fields have exactly two ideals (0) and the whole field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of basic arithmetic maps (topology exercises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard arithmetic maps on real numbers are continuous: subtraction − : R×R → R is continuous; division ÷ : R×R_{>0} → R is continuous; similar statements for addition and multiplication (implicit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises include: exhibit f:R→R continuous only at 0; show strictly increasing f:R→R must be continuous at some point; discuss continuity of 1/x (answer: 1/x is continuous on its domain R\{0}, but not defined/continuous at 0). The product space uses product metric.
